transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist here. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi. Well, I teach high school, and... I'm here because I just can't stop focusing on my face. When I look at the lesson videos I have to make for my classes, all I can see is this crooked, swollen-looking side of my face. It's just... once I notice it, I feel like the students, their parents, the other staff, they must all be staring right at it instead of listening to a single word I'm actually saying.

When you're not looking at the videos or thinking about how you look on camera, do you actually notice this crookedness or swelling in your face when you look in the mirror normally, or is it mainly something you see in the recorded videos?

It's... no, it's not just the videos. I definitely see it in the mirror, too. Whenever I look in the bathroom mirror at home, I see the exact same swelling and crookedness. The videos just make it harder to deal with because I know my students are watching them, but yeah, I see it normally all the time.
Have other people, like your family, friends, or colleagues, ever mentioned anything about swelling or crookedness on that side of your face, or do they say it looks normal to them?

No, nobody has ever said anything about it. If I bring it up, my wife just tells me I look fine and that she doesn't see what I'm talking about. But... I mean, people usually don't point out things like that to your face, right? They probably just notice it and try to be polite. But no, no one has ever actually mentioned it to me.
How much time each day would you say you spend checking your face in mirrors, or thinking about this swelling and crookedness? And has this been affecting your ability to teach or do your job?

I'd say I probably spend a few hours a day just checking the mirror or looking at my phone camera, trying to see how bad it is. And I'm thinking about it almost constantly. 

As for my job... yeah, it's definitely affecting things. I've fallen really behind on my lesson planning. I used to do mentoring and coach the basketball team, but I've had to pull back because I just can't get my main work finished on time anymore. The administration has actually started documenting my missed deadlines and issues with covering my classes. Honestly, I'm pretty worried I might lose my job over this. It's just so hard to focus on anything else.

When you're thinking about this swelling and crookedness on your face, are you mainly worried about how it looks and what others think of your appearance, or are you also concerned that something might be medically wrong with your face—like an infection, tumor, or some kind of disease?

I don't think it's a medical thing. I mean, I'm not worried about a tumor or a disease or anything like that. It's really just about how it looks. I just... I hate how it looks, and I'm worried about everyone else seeing it, especially when I have to stand up in front of a classroom of teenagers or when they watch those videos. So, yeah, it's just the appearance that bothers me.

Besides checking the mirror and looking at photos of yourself, do you find yourself picking at your skin, pulling out your hair, or biting your nails—especially when you're stressed or anxious about your appearance?

No, I don't really do any of that. I don't pick at my skin or pull my hair out or bite my nails. It's... it really is just the mirrors and the photos on my phone. That's what I get stuck doing when I get anxious about it, but not the other stuff.

When you feel the urge to check the mirror or your phone camera, does it feel like something you absolutely have to do to relieve anxiety or tension—like you can't resist it—or is it more that you're choosing to check because you're worried about how you look?

I'm not really sure how to answer that, to be honest. I haven't really thought about the difference. 

I just know that I'm worried about my face, so I look. I don't know if it's... like an urge I absolutely can't resist, or if I'm just choosing to check because I'm anxious about how bad it is. It all just kind of blends together for me. I just get worried, and then I check the mirror or my phone. I don't really know which one of those it is.

If you tried to stop yourself from checking the mirror or your phone camera right now, do you think you could resist that urge and wait, say, 30 minutes before checking again—or does it feel completely impossible to hold back?

I don't think I could wait 30 minutes. If I tried to stop myself... I mean, the anxiety would just build up too much. It feels like I absolutely have to look to see how bad it is. So, no, holding back for that long feels pretty much impossible.

When you do check the mirror or your phone camera, does looking at your face actually make the anxiety go away for a little while, or does the worry and anxiety stay pretty much the same no matter how many times you check?

No, it doesn't really make the anxiety go away. If anything, it just makes me do it more. 

Like, with my job—I teach high school—if I have to post a recorded lesson or get on a video call for a parent conference, I just... I get stuck. I keep changing the camera angle, trying to find a way where it doesn't look so bad. I'll replay clips of myself over and over, or I'll sit there covering parts of my face with my hand to see if it helps. I end up re-recording the whole thing so many times that I miss my prep periods. I've even ended up being late for my actual classes because I'm just stuck doing that, and the worry never really goes away.
